_link.title: I can explain how orientation affects whether a collision is successful

toLevel2.stem: In collision theory, what does 'orientation' refer to?
toLevel2.answer: The alignment of particles when they collide
distractors: The speed of particles as they approach each other
The distance between particles before collision
The temperature of the surrounding environment

toLevel2.stem: What happens when particles collide with sufficient energy but in the wrong orientation?
distractors: They react but form different products
They lose all their kinetic energy
They combine to form a catalyst

toLevel2.stem: For a collision to be successful, particles must collide with correct orientation so that:
toLevel2.answer: bonds can break and new bonds can form
distractors: the particles can absorb more energy
the particles can slow down sufficiently
the activation energy can be eliminated

toLevel2.stem: Which of the following is a condition of collision theory alongside sufficient energy?
distractors: High temperature of the system
Presence of a catalyst in solution
Low pressure in the container

toLevel2.stem: When two molecules collide in incorrect orientation, the result is:
distractors: a successful reaction every time
an increase in activation energy
the formation of a transition state

toLevel2.stem: A collision can be unsuccessful even if the particles have enough energy, due to incorrect orientation.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: All collisions between particles with sufficient energy result in a successful reaction.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with the correct {{blank:1}} so that {{blank:2}} can break and form.
distractors: temperature
atoms
pressure
electrons

toLevel2.stem: When particles collide in the wrong alignment, they simply {{blank:1}} apart and no {{blank:2}} occurs.
distractors: split
collision
break
transfer

toLevel2.stem: Orientation refers to the {{blank:1}} alignment of particles during a {{blank:2}}.
distractors: thermal
reaction
magnetic
transfer

toLevel3.stem: Why can reactions have a low success rate even when particles have enough energy?
toLevel3.answer: Many collisions occur in the wrong orientation
distractors: The particles are too large to collide effectively
The activation energy increases during the reaction
The temperature drops each time a collision occurs

toLevel3.stem: How does incorrect orientation prevent a reaction from occurring?
toLevel3.answer: The reactive parts of the molecules do not come into contact
distractors: The molecules lose their kinetic energy before colliding
The molecules form a stable intermediate that cannot decompose
The molecules transfer energy to the surroundings instead

toLevel3.stem: In the lock-and-key analogy for orientation, what does the 'key fitting into the lock' represent?
toLevel3.answer: Particles aligning correctly so bonds can break and form
distractors: Particles reaching the correct temperature to react
Particles having the minimum activation energy needed
Particles being in the same phase during the collision

toLevel3.stem: Why is orientation particularly important for reactions involving larger molecules?
toLevel3.answer: Larger molecules have more possible alignments, reducing the chance of correct orientation
distractors: Larger molecules always have higher activation energies than smaller ones
Larger molecules cannot collide with sufficient energy at any temperature
Larger molecules do not follow the rules of collision theory at all

toLevel3.stem: What is the relationship between orientation and the formation of products?
toLevel3.answer: Correct orientation allows the necessary bonds to break and new bonds to form
distractors: Correct orientation increases the kinetic energy of colliding particles
Correct orientation reduces the activation energy of the reaction
Correct orientation ensures all collisions produce the transition state

toLevel3.stem: Gases often have a low percentage of successful collisions despite having enough energy. How does orientation help explain this?
toLevel3.answer: Gas particles move freely and often collide in misaligned geometries
distractors: Gas particles always collide at speeds too high for reactions
Gas particles are too far apart to ever meet in the correct way
Gas particles lose their orientation as temperature increases

toLevel3.stem: Orientation explains why not every high-energy collision results in a reaction.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Even with sufficient energy, a collision is unsuccessful if the {{blank:1}} parts of the molecules do not come into {{blank:2}}.
distractors: outer
motion
neutral
solution

toLevel3.stem: Gases often have a low percentage of successful collisions because particles move {{blank:1}} and frequently collide in {{blank:2}} alignments.
distractors: slowly
correct
rarely
parallel

toLevel3.stem: Orientation is one of the three conditions of collision theory, along with sufficient {{blank:1}} and the particles actually {{blank:2}}.
distractors: mass
dissolving
pressure
separating

toLevel4.stem: Two XY molecules collide end-to-end so that the X atoms face each other. Which outcome is most likely?
toLevel4.answer: A successful collision forming X–X and Y–Y bonds
distractors: An unsuccessful collision because the energy is too low
A successful collision forming X–Y and X–Y bonds
An unsuccessful collision because XY molecules cannot react

toLevel4.stem: A student observes that only 1 in every 1000 collisions between two gas molecules results in a reaction, even though most collisions have enough energy. What is the most likely explanation?
toLevel4.answer: Most collisions occur in the wrong orientation
distractors: The gas molecules are too small to react with each other
The activation energy is zero for this particular reaction
The system is at too high a temperature for reactions

toLevel4.stem: In a reaction between molecule A–B and molecule C–D, the A end of A–B must contact the C end of C–D. If A–B approaches with the B end facing C–D, what occurs?
toLevel4.answer: No reaction — the molecules bounce apart
distractors: A reaction forming B–C and A–D products
A reaction forming A–C and B–D products
The molecules combine to form A–B–C–D

toLevel4.stem: A chemist is studying a reaction with a very low success rate. The activation energy is low and collisions are frequent. Which factor most likely limits the reaction rate?
toLevel4.answer: The orientation requirement is very specific
distractors: The temperature is too high for the reaction
The particles are in a closed system
The concentration of reactants is too high

toLevel4.stem: A student models a collision using two bar magnets. In which scenario would the magnets 'react' (stick together)?
toLevel4.answer: When the north pole of one faces the south pole of the other
distractors: When both north poles face each other head-on
When both south poles face each other head-on
When the magnets are placed side by side facing the same way

toLevel4.stem: In an industrial process, a reaction between two complex molecules has a low yield. Scientists determine that the molecules have many possible collision orientations. How does this explain the low yield?
toLevel4.answer: Only a few orientations allow the correct bonds to break and form
distractors: Complex molecules have no activation energy to overcome
Complex molecules always collide with insufficient energy
Complex molecules cannot collide in a closed system

toLevel4.stem: A student sets up two identical reactions but stirs one vigorously. Both have the same temperature and concentration. If the stirred reaction is slightly faster, what has stirring affected?
distractors: The orientation of every collision in the mixture
The activation energy of the stirred reaction
The molecular geometry of the reactant particles

toLevel4.stem: If molecule A–B must collide with the {{blank:1}} end of molecule C–D facing the A end, any other alignment results in an {{blank:2}} collision.
distractors: D
exothermic
B
endothermic

toLevel4.stem: A reaction with many possible collision geometries but only one correct alignment will have a {{blank:1}} proportion of {{blank:2}} collisions.
distractors: high
energetic
equal
frequent

toLevel4.stem: When a low activation energy reaction still has a low success rate, the most likely limiting factor is the {{blank:1}} {{blank:2}}.
distractors: energy
barrier
collision
frequency

toLevel5.stem: A reaction has a low activation energy and high collision frequency but a very low rate. Which analysis best accounts for this observation?
toLevel5.answer: The orientation requirement is extremely specific, so very few collisions succeed
distractors: The low activation energy prevents most particles from reacting at all
High collision frequency always results in high reaction rates regardless
The reaction must be endothermic which makes it inherently slow

toLevel5.stem: Two reactions have the same activation energy and collision frequency. Reaction A has a simpler orientation requirement than Reaction B. Which statement is best supported?
toLevel5.answer: Reaction A will be faster due to a higher proportion of correctly oriented collisions
distractors: Reaction B will be faster because complex orientation lowers the energy barrier
Both reactions will proceed at the same rate since Ea and frequency are equal
Reaction A will be slower because simpler molecules collide less effectively

toLevel5.stem: Increasing temperature raises the proportion of successful collisions. Does this improvement relate to orientation, energy, or both?
toLevel5.answer: Primarily energy — more particles exceed Ea, but orientation requirements stay the same
distractors: Primarily orientation — higher temperature aligns particles more correctly
Both equally — temperature improves orientation and energy by the same amount
Neither — temperature only increases collision frequency, not success rate

toLevel5.stem: A student claims: 'If we could control particle orientation, we could make any reaction instantaneous.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — particles would still need sufficient energy to overcome the activation energy
distractors: Correct — orientation is the only factor that limits reaction rate
Incorrect — controlling orientation would stop all collisions from occurring
Correct — energy is automatically provided when orientation is correct

toLevel5.stem: In a reaction between two asymmetric molecules, there are 12 possible collision geometries but only 1 leads to product formation. What fraction of collisions with sufficient energy will be successful?
distractors: Approximately 12 in 12
Approximately 1 in 2
Approximately 6 in 12

toLevel5.stem: A peer states: 'Adding a catalyst improves particle orientation.' Is this an accurate description of how catalysts work?
toLevel5.answer: No — catalysts provide an alternative pathway with lower Ea, not better orientation
distractors: Yes — catalysts align particles in the correct orientation for reaction
No — catalysts only increase the temperature of the reaction mixture
Yes — catalysts physically rotate particles into the correct position

toLevel5.stem: Consider the four possible outcomes of a particle collision. Which combination leads to a successful reaction?
distractors: Incorrect orientation and sufficient energy
Correct orientation and insufficient energy
Incorrect orientation and insufficient energy

toLevel5.stem: A student says: 'Increasing concentration improves the chance of correct orientation in each collision.' Evaluate this statement.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — concentration increases collision frequency but does not change orientation probability per collision
distractors: Correct — more particles means better alignment in every collision
Incorrect — concentration has no effect on reaction rate whatsoever
Correct — higher concentration forces particles into correct alignment

toLevel5.stem: Increasing temperature increases reaction rate mainly by providing more particles with sufficient {{blank:1}}, while the {{blank:2}} requirement remains unchanged.
distractors: mass
temperature
speed
frequency

toLevel5.stem: Of the four collision outcomes, only the combination of correct {{blank:1}} and sufficient {{blank:2}} results in a successful reaction.
distractors: temperature
pressure
frequency
mass
